title: Experimental Ebola Vaccines Race Ahead as Congo Death Toll Nears 1,000
excerpt: With no approved treatments for the Bundibugyo strain, Africa CDC is preparing a cross-protection trial for health workers while developers including Oxford and Serum Institute of India push toward clinical trials.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • DRC's Ebola outbreak has reached 2,473 cases and 999 deaths, the fastest-growing on record.
  • 121 health workers have been infected, with 36 fatalities, highlighting urgent vaccine needs.
  • Africa CDC plans a Phase-2 trial for cross-protection against Bundibugyo using existing vaccines.
  • Developers like Oxford and Serum Institute are racing to create Bundibugyo-specific vaccines with $50 million support.

Africa CDC is preparing to launch a Phase-2 clinical trial testing whether existing Ebola vaccines can provide cross-protection against the Bundibugyo strain, as the Democratic Republic of Congo's outbreak approaches 1,000 deaths with no approved vaccine or treatment available.

Death Toll Approaches Grim Milestone

The DRC outbreak, declared on May 15, has recorded 2,473 confirmed cases and 999 deaths as of July 20, according to the country's Ministry of Health. It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record — previous outbreaks, including the 2013–2016 West Africa epidemic that killed more than 11,000 people, took around eight months to reach 1,000 deaths.

Ituri province remains the epicenter, accounting for more than 90 percent of cases and 80 percent of deaths, according to WHO Incident Manager Dr. Thierno Baldé. The outbreak has spread to four additional provinces: North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, and Tshopo. About 80 percent of new infections are linked to unknown transmission chains, and response operations have been hampered by attacks on health facilities and strikes over unpaid salaries.

A Cross-Protection Strategy for Health Workers

At least 121 health workers have been infected during the outbreak, with 36 dead, according to Bloomberg. Africa CDC is working with Médecins Sans Frontières to test whether Merck's Ervebo — licensed against the Zaire strain — followed by an experimental Sudan Ebola vaccine from the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative, can offer partial protection against Bundibugyo.

The agency expects to submit the trial design to its executive committee this week, with the trial potentially starting within two weeks. Africa CDC plans to contribute $500,000 to launch the study.

“We intend to do this under a phase-2 clinical trial among a small cohort of healthcare workers, where any level of protection could provide benefits to them.”

— Africa CDC

The approach draws on research from the University of Texas Medical Branch, where macaques given sequential vaccines against the Sudan and Zaire strains survived exposure to the Bundibugyo virus, while most animals receiving both vaccines simultaneously did not.

WHO has cautioned against broader deployment outside controlled settings. Vasee Moorthy, who leads WHO's R&D work on epidemic threats, warned that broader use “could generate a false sense of security among affected communities, potentially undermining trust in proven public health measures.”

Multiple developers are racing to create Bundibugyo-specific vaccines. IAVI is advancing an rVSV-based candidate and expects doses to be ready for human trials by the end of 2026, according to Reuters. Oxford University and India's Serum Institute are developing ChAdOx1, built on the same platform behind the Oxford-AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine. Moderna is developing an mRNA-based shot with CEPI support, and Public Health Vaccines is developing a candidate similar to Ervebo.

Gavi has committed $50 million through its First Response Fund to accelerate vaccine access, with preference given to production in Africa. On July 2, WHO added the first diagnostic test for Bundibugyo virus to its Emergency Use Listing, and patient enrollment began in a trial to identify the first effective treatments.

India's Serum Institute and Diaspora Stakes

Serum Institute of India's involvement extends the manufacturing partnership it built with Oxford during COVID-19. The Pune-based firm, one of the world's largest vaccine makers, could play a central role in scaling production. For India's diaspora across East and Central Africa, the outbreak carries direct risks — Uganda has reported cases linked to the DRC outbreak, though none since June 21.

What's Next

Africa CDC's executive committee is expected to review the cross-protection trial this week. WHO's advisory group has called for prioritizing experimental antibodies, antivirals, and vaccines.

“If we do not stop this outbreak today, it could become one of the worst Ebola outbreaks the world has ever documented.”

— Dr. Jean Kaseya, Africa CDC Director-General
